newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Taiwan, China shipping deal set but details murky.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan, China shipping deal set but details murky.

text.p: Taiwan and China negotiators said they reached an understanding on Wednesday in unofficial talks in Hong Kong that could end a decades-old ban on direct shipping across the Taiwan Strait.
Non-government negotiators said they had reached a consensus allowing authorised shipping companies to seek approval from China to sail directly between the island and the mainland.

"Following this meeting between the two civilian associations, and with our permission and approval to allow operation of the Kaohsiung to Fuzhou and Xiamen route, operators can immediately submit applications to China to start business," Lin Hsing-shan, head of the Taiwan delegation, told reporters.
Kaohsiung is Taiwan's main southern port, which lies 300 km (185 miles) east of the mainland's southeastern ports of Fuzhou and Xiamen.

Taiwan government radio quoted Lin, chairman of the Nationalist-ruled island's Evergreen Marine, as saying shipping companies that already had been approved by Taiwan for Kaohsiung, Fuzhou and Xiamen now could apply to the mainland.
Fourteen Taiwan and foreign firms had done so, officials said.
Neither side gave any explicit indication of how Beijing would respond to Taiwan shippers' applications and no mention was made of provisions for mainland shippers.
Beijing's negotiator in the one-day closed-door talks, Meng Guangju of China's state-sanctioned Straits Shipping Exchange Association, gave an upbeat but vague assessment of the talks.
"Following the expansion of cross-strait exchanges and the result of consultations on the direct link, there will be a gradual opening," Meng told reporters.
Cross-straits shipping now is routed through Hong Kong, an arrangement whose future becomes clouded after July 1 when the British colony reverts to Chinese rule.
Taiwan radio said foreign-flagged ships might begin sailing direct routes as early as March or April.
Taiwan political analyst Tim Ting was sceptical, noting that neither side appeared to be willing to make concessions on their strikingly different visions of how direct shipping might work.
"I don't see the possibility that China will withdraw or step back a little bit or that Taiwan will step back a little bit," Ting, a professor at National Taiwan University, told Reuters in Taipei.

Taiwan has proposed that initial direct sailings involve only ships flying third-country flags and that cargoes from the mainland be handled at offshore transshipment centres that lie outside Taiwan customs. Taiwan shippers could still benefit because many are registered overseas.
Beijing, which regards Taiwan as a rebel-held province, sees the issue entirely as a domestic matter and promulgated rules to that effect on August 20.
Beijing would not welcome ships flying the flag of the exiled Republic of China government, which took refuge on Taiwan in 1949 after its civil war defeat on the mainland.
Taipei responded icily to Beijing's rules, saying at the time that they were "mingled with sensitive political issues".
Taiwan is loath to take steps that could be seen as conferring legitimacy on the communist People's Republic or recognising its sovereignty.
Taiwan's business community nonetheless is eager to deepen already flourishing business ties with the mainland by ending Taipei's ban on official contacts, which adds to costs.
Taipei has banned direct links with the mainland since Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist republic fled to Taiwan.

In its drive to become an Asia-Pacific business hub, Taiwan proposed in 1995 to set up an offshore transshipment centre at Kaohsiung from which ships would be allowed to sail directly between Taiwan and China -- but insists that mainland cargoes not be allowed inside Taiwan's customs.
